analysis.one_liner: Caps how far back the government can collect oil and gas royalties from federal-land drillers.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by voice vote, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and President Clinton signed it into law as Public Law 104-185 on August 13, 1996.
analysis.plain_summary: This law rewrites how the federal government collects oil and gas royalties from companies drilling on public lands and offshore. It sets a seven-year limit on how far back the government can pursue unpaid royalties, imposes deadlines that automatically rule in the company's favor if the agency misses them on smaller claims, and pays companies interest on their own overpayments. It also lets states take over federal royalty audits with federal reimbursement and gives accounting relief to operators of low-producing wells. Indian lands are excluded and keep the stricter pre-existing rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that hold federal and offshore leases. They get a hard seven-year cutoff on royalty claims that survives only if the government signs a written tolling agreement, issues a subpoena, or proves fraud; a 33-month deadline for the agency to decide appeals, with claims under $10,000 automatically decided for the company if the deadline is missed; interest paid by the Treasury on the companies' own overpayments; a bar on the agency demanding data like allowances and payor information; optional prepayment of royalties and lighter accounting for low-producing wells; and the option of having a state, with federal money, handle audits and collections instead of the Interior Department.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies on federal leases

how_it_helps.text: Sets a seven-year statute of limitations on any royalty claim or demand, after which the government cannot pursue, audit, or bill for the obligation; the clock stops only for a written tolling agreement, a qualifying subpoena, or intentional misrepresentation or concealment by the company.

Requires the Interior Department to issue a final decision on any administrative appeal within 33 months; if it misses the deadline, any claim under $10,000 is automatically decided in the company's favor.
Entitles companies to interest, paid by the Treasury, on royalty overpayments, and gives companies up to six years to adjust and request refunds of overpayments.

Allows any state to apply to take over federal royalty inspections, audits, report processing, and collection demands within its borders, with the Secretary of the Interior required to compensate the state for its costs.

Gives relief to marginal wells — those producing under roughly 15 barrels of oil or 90 thousand cubic feet of gas per well per day — including prepayment of royalties in a lump sum and lighter accounting, reporting, and auditing requirements.
Limits the data the Secretary can require and waives interest where an agency determination is delayed, reducing compliance burdens on lessees.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury and the states. Federal onshore royalties are split roughly 50/50 with the states under general mineral-leasing law, so any underpayment the seven-year cutoff bars from collection is revenue neither government ever sees. The law also pays companies interest on overpayments and requires refunds, with the portion attributable to money already disbursed deducted from states' shares and the Reclamation Fund. For companies that underpaid in the past, the difference between what was owed and what the seven-year window allows is a loss absorbed by the public.

drawbacks.text: The seven-year cutoff bars the government from collecting older underpayments — the bill was written amid disputes over oil companies underpaying federal royalties — so money owed by lessees before the window closes is simply never collected by the Treasury or the states.

If the agency misses the 33-month decision deadline on an appeal, any claim under $10,000 is automatically decided for the company, converting bureaucratic delay into a windfall rather than requiring the merits to be heard.
Refunds of overpayments and the interest paid on them are drawn partly from amounts already disbursed to states and the Reclamation Fund, reducing those shares when companies overpaid in the past.

The law repeals section 10 of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act governing federal gas sales; the original version of the bill described this change as lifting the prohibition on selling federal gas to the public for less than fair market value.

Delegating audits and collections to states — whose budgets and politics are intertwined with the local industry — could soften enforcement, though the Secretary retains authority to revoke a delegation and to step in when a state fails to issue a demand.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's defenders had a real case: federal royalty disputes in the mid-1990s dragged on for years, audits reached back indefinitely, and the agency sat on appeals, so hard deadlines and a defined cutoff give companies and auditors genuine certainty. But the tradeoff is one-sided in design. The rules that protect companies — the seven-year bar, the automatic win on sub-$10,000 claims when the agency is late, interest on overpayments — all shift collection risk from the industry to the Treasury and the states, while the offsetting protections (revocable delegation, fraud tolling, a new assessment for chronic erroneous reporting) are hedged and enforcement-dependent. The telling detail is that Indian lands were carved out entirely and kept under the stricter old rules, an implicit acknowledgment that the new framework is weaker for those it covers.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House by voice vote and the Senate by unanimous consent with no amendments, and President Clinton signed it into law on August 13, 1996.

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Calvert introduced the bill on June 30, 1995. It was referred to the House Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which held hearings in July 1995.

The subcommittee approved an amended version by voice vote in February 1996, and the full committee ordered the bill reported on a 20-7 vote on March 28, 1996, formally reporting it with amendments on July 11, 1996.
On July 16, 1996, Calvert moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill — a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial measures that bypasses amendments — and the House agreed by voice vote.
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by unanimous consent on August 2, 1996, meaning no senator objected.
President Clinton signed the bill on August 13, 1996, and it became Public Law 104-185.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies producing from federal lands and the Outer Continental Shelf came out ahead: they won a hard seven-year limit on royalty claims, deadlines that default in their favor when the agency is slow, Treasury-paid interest on overpayments, and lighter reporting requirements. Producing states also gained the option of taking over audits with federal reimbursement. The public bears the uncollected underpayments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies on federal leases

sides.party_line_note: The bill carried cosponsors from both parties, passed the House by voice vote and the Senate by unanimous consent, and was signed by a Democratic president; the only recorded opposition was the 7 no votes out of 27 cast in the Resources Committee markup.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with federal and offshore leases
industries.note: The law caps how far back the government can pursue, audit, and bill them for unpaid royalties at seven years, pays them interest on overpayments, imposes decision deadlines that default in their favor on smaller claims, and strips data and enforcement requirements. Their gain comes directly out of federal and state royalty revenue.

Wells averaging under about 15 barrels of oil or 90 thousand cubic feet of gas per day get optional royalty prepayment and reduced accounting, reporting, and auditing. The relief lowers the public's collections from these leases but is aimed at keeping marginal wells economically viable rather than plugged.

States can take over federal royalty audits, report processing, and collections within their borders, with the Interior Department required to reimburse their costs — real authority and funding. But states receive roughly half of federal onshore royalties, so the same seven-year cutoff and company refunds also cut into their revenue.
